issues.legal_issue: A public-interest organization with a genuine and particular concern in the use of public property may challenge government allotments of that property.
material_facts: The petitioner was a society formed by retired civil servants, journalists and other residents, and challenged government housing arrangements said to affect public property and the State exchequer.
The petition disclosed no personal grievance or oblique motive, and the court considered the concern raised to be just and proper.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner had locus standi and the public-interest petition was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 32, a petitioner with a special interest or a concern deeper than that of a busybody may have standing to raise a justiciable public issue. The Court relied on Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union (Regd.) Sindri v. Union of India, (1981) 1 SCC 568, and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981 Supp SCC 87.

predicates.public_interest_petition: An organization brings a public-interest proceeding challenging the use or allocation of public resources.
predicates.organization_special_interest: The organization has a particular concern in the subject matter beyond the general interest shared by the public at large.
predicates.no_oblique_motive: The organization brought the proceeding without an improper personal or collateral motive.

issues.definition: When an organization brings a public-interest petition about a matter in which it has a particular concern and does so without an improper motive, the petition is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Executive rules cannot confer lifetime government housing on former ministers when the governing statute limits their entitlement to housing during office and for a short period after leaving office.
material_facts: A state statute governing ministers' salaries and perquisites entitled each minister, including the chief minister, to an official residence during office and for fifteen days afterward.
The state made non-statutory executive rules providing a government residence to former chief ministers for life.
The rules thus extended housing beyond the statutory entitlement and gave former chief ministers a benefit not provided to other constitutional officeholders.
The state relied on security needs for some former chief ministers, but the Court noted that central government guidelines addressed accommodation for protected persons.
issues.conclusion: The executive rules were invalid insofar as they conflicted with the statute, and the state could not permit former chief ministers to occupy government accommodation after the statutory post-office period.
issues.legal_principle: Article 164(5) of the Constitution and Entry 40 of List II of the Seventh Schedule empower the state legislature to determine ministers' salaries and allowances. Section 4 of the Uttar Pradesh Ministers (Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1981 provided official residence during office and for fifteen days thereafter. Executive instructions cannot prevail over a contrary statutory provision. The Court also found no reasonable basis for the preferential benefit under Article 14. It referred to S.D. Bandi v. Karnataka SRTC, (2013) 12 SCC 631, concerning unauthorized occupation; it did not decide the broader accommodation issue discussed in Shiv Sagar Tiwari v. Union of India, (1997) 1 SCC 444, because that issue was not challenged in this proceeding.

predicates.challenge_to_executive_housing_rule: A proceeding challenges an executive rule that grants government housing to former officeholders.
predicates.former_ministers_get_government_housing: The executive rule grants former ministers government housing after they leave office.
predicates.statute_limits_official_housing_after_of: A governing statute limits official housing to the period in office and a defined short period afterward.
predicates.executive_rule_exceeds_statutory_entitle: The executive rule grants housing beyond the entitlement fixed by the governing statute.

issues.definition: If a challenged executive housing rule grants former ministers housing beyond the period allowed by statute, the rule is invalid to the extent of that conflict.

issues.legal_issue: Government property cannot be allotted to private bodies without legal authority and adequate consideration, and an unauthorized allotment must be ended.
material_facts: Government bungalows had been allotted to private trusts, societies or organizations when there was no statutory provision authorizing the allotments.
The allotments were made without adequate market rent or other adequate consideration.
The Court directed the state to take possession of the premises and recover appropriate rent for the period of unauthorized occupation.
issues.conclusion: The allotments were unjustified and could not be upheld; the state had to end them, take possession of the premises and recover appropriate rent for unauthorized occupation.
issues.legal_principle: The state may not fritter away public property in favour of private persons or bodies without adequate consideration. In the absence of statutory authority, allotments of government property to private bodies without adequate market consideration are unlawful. The Court also referred to S.D. Bandi v. Karnataka SRTC, (2013) 12 SCC 631, on the consequences of unauthorized occupation of government accommodation.

rule.if: challenge_to_public_property_allocation and private_bodies_received_public_property and no_authorizing_law_at_allotment and no_adequate_market_consideration

predicates.challenge_to_public_property_allocation: A proceeding challenges the allocation of government property to private bodies.
predicates.private_bodies_received_public_property: Private trusts, societies, organizations or other private bodies received government property.
predicates.no_authorizing_law_at_allotment: No law authorized the allocation when it was made.
predicates.no_adequate_market_consideration: The recipients did not provide adequate market consideration for the property.

issues.definition: When private bodies receive government property without legal authority and adequate market consideration, the allotment must end and appropriate rent must be recovered.
